Volpone or the fox

Ben Jonson — EMOTHE0265_VolponeOrTheFox

THE PERSONS OF THE PLAY

  • Volpone, a magnifico
  • Mosca, his parasite
  • Voltore, an advocate
  • Corbaccio, an old gentleman
  • Corvino, a merchant
  • Avocatori, four magistrates
  • Notario, the registrer
  • Nano, a dwarf
  • Castrone, an eunuch
  • Grege, (the crowd)
  • Sir Politic Would-be, a knight
  • Peregrine, a gentleman traveler
  • Bonario, son to Corbaccio
  • Fine Madam Would-be, Sir Politic’s wife
  • Celia, the merchant's wife
  • Commandatori, officers of justice
  • Mercatori, three merchants
  • Androgyno, a hermaphrodite
  • Servitori, a servant
  • Women, two

The scene: Venice.

ACT 1

SCENE 1

(Enter Volpone and Mosca.)

VOLPONE

1Good morning to the day; and next, my gold! –
2Open the shrine, that I may see my saint.
3[Mosca reveals the treasure.] Hail the world's soul, and mine! more glad than is
4The teeming earth to see the longed-for sun
5Peep through the horns of the celestial Ram,
6Am I, to view thy splendour darkening his;
7That lying here, amongst my other hoards,
8Show'st like a flame by night, or like the day
9Struck out of chaos, when all darkness fled
10Unto the center. O thou son of Sol,
11But brighter than thy father, let me kiss,
12With adoration, thee, and every relic
13Of sacred treasure in this blessed room.
14Well did wise poets, by thy glorious name,
15Title that age which they would have the best;
16Thou being the best of things, and far transcending
17All style of joy, in children, parents, friends,
18Or any other waking dream on earth:
19Thy looks when they to Venus did ascribe,
20They should have given her twenty thousand Cupids;
21Such are thy beauties and our loves! Dear saint,
22Riches, the dumb god, that giv'st all men tongues,
23Thou canst do naught, and yet mak'st men do all things;
24The price of souls; even hell, with thee to boot,
25Is made worth heaven. Thou art virtue, fame,
26Honour, and all things else. Who can get thee,
27He shall be noble valiant, honest, wise –

MOSCA

28And what he will, sir. Riches are in fortune
29A greater good than wisdom is in nature.

VOLPONE

30True, my beloved Mosca. Yet I glory
31More in the cunning purchase of my wealth,
32Than in the glad possession, since I gain
33No common way; I use no trade, no venture;
34I wound no earth with plough-shares, fat no beasts,
35To feed the shambles; have no mills for iron,
36Oil, corn, or men, to grind them into powder;
37I blow no subtle glass; expose no ships
38To threat'nings of the furrow-faced sea;
39I turn no monies in the public bank,
40Nor usure private.

MOSCA

Nor usure private. No, sir, nor devour
41Soft prodigals. You shall have some will swallow
42A melting heir as glibly as your Dutch
43Will pills of butter, and ne'er purge for it;
44Tear forth the fathers of poor families
45Out of their beds, and coffin them alive
46In some kind clasping prison, where their bones
47May be forthcoming, when the flesh is rotten:
48But your sweet nature doth abhor these courses;
49You loathe the widow's or the orphan's tears
50Should wash your pavements, or their piteous cries
51Ring in your roofs, and beat the air for vengeance.

VOLPONE

52Right, Mosca, I do lothe it.

MOSCA

Right, Mosca, I do lothe it. And besides, sir,
53You are not like the thresher that doth stand
54With a huge flail, watching a heap of corn,
55And, hungry, dares not taste the smallest grain,
56But feeds on mallows, and such bitter herbs;
57Nor like the merchant, who hath filled his vaults
58With Romagnia, and rich Candian wines,
59Yet drinks the lees of Lombard's vinegar:
60You will lie not in straw, whilst moths and worms
61Feed on your sumptuous hangings and soft beds;
62You know the use of riches, and dare give now
63From that bright heap, to me, your poor observer,
64Or to your dwarf, or your hermaphrodite,
65Your eunuch, or what other household trifle
66Your pleasure allows maintenance –

VOLPONE

Your pleasure allows maintenance – Hold thee, Mosca,
67[Gives him money.] Take of my hand; thou strik'st on truth in all,
68And they are envious term thee parasite.
69Call forth my dwarf, my eunuch, and my fool,
70And let them make me sport.
And let them make me sport. [Exit Mosca.] What should I do
71But cocker up my genius, and live free
72To all delights my fortune calls me to?
73I have no wife, no parent, child, ally,
74To give my substance to; but whom I make
75Must be my heir: and this makes men observe me:
76This draws new clients daily to my house,
77Women and men of every sex and age,
78That bring me presents, send me plate, coin, jewels,
79With hope that when I die (which they expect
80Each greedy minute) it shall then return
81Ten-fold upon them; whilst some, covetous
82Above the rest, seek to engross me whole,
83And counter-work the one unto the other,
84Contend in gifts as they would seem in love:
85All which I suffer, playing with their hopes,
86And am content to coin them into profit,
87And look upon their kindness, and take more,
88And look on that; still bearing them in hand,
89Letting the cherry knock against their lips,
90And draw it by their mouths and back again. – How now!

ACT 1, Scene 2

(Enter Mosca with Nano, Androgyno, and Castrone.)

NANO

1Now, room for fresh gamester, who do will you to know,
2They do bring you neither play nor university show;
3And therefore do entreat you, that whatsoever they rehearse,
4May not fare a whit the worse, for the false pace of the verse.
5If you wonder at this, you will wonder more ere we pass,
6For know, here is enclosed the soul of Pythagoras,
7That juggler divine, as hereafter shall follow;
8Which soul, fast and loose, sir, came first from Apollo,
9And was breathed into Aethalides, Mercurius, his son,
10Where it had the gift to remember all that ever was done.
11From thence it fled forth, and made quick transmigration
12To goldilocked Euphorbus, who was killed in good fashion,
13At the siege of old Troy, by the cuckold of Sparta.
14Hermotimus was next (I find it in my charta)
15To whom it did pass, where no sooner it was missing
16But with one Pyrrhus of Delos it learned to go a-fishing;
17And thence did it enter the sophist of Greece.
18From Pythagore, she went into a beautiful piece,
19Hight Aspasia, the meretrix; and the next toss of her
20Was again of a whore, she became a philosopher,
21Crates the cynic, as itself doth relate it:
22Since kings, knights, and beggars, knaves, lords, and
23fools gat it,
24Besides ox and ass, camel, mule, goat, and brock,
25In all which it hath spoke, as in the cobbler’s cock.
26But I come not here to discourse of that matter,
27Or his one, two, or three, or his great oath, “By quarter!”
28His musics, his trigon, his golden thigh,
29Or his telling how elements shift, but I
30Would ask, how of late thou hast suffered translation,
31And shifted thy coat in these days of reformation.

ANDROGYNO

32Like one of the reformed, a fool, as you see,
33Counting all old doctrine heresy.

NANO

34But not on thine own forbid meats hast thou ventured?

ANDROGYNO

35On fish, when first a Carthusian I entered.

NANO

36Why, then thy dogmatical silence hath left thee?

ANDROGYNO

37Of that an obstreperous lawyer bereft me.

NANO

38O wonderful change, when sir lawyer forsook thee!
39For Pythagore's sake, what body then took thee?

ANDROGYNO

40A good dull mule.

NANO

A good dull mule. And how, by that means,
41Thou wert brought to allow of the eating of beans?

ANDROGYNO

42Yes.

NANO

Yes. But from the mule into whom didst thou pass?

ANDROGYNO

43Into a very strange beast, by some writers called an ass;
44By others, a precise, pure, illuminate brother,
45Of those devour flesh, and sometimes one another;
46And will drop you forth a libel, or a sanctified lie,
47Betwixt every spoonful of a nativity-pie.

NANO

48Now quit thee, for heaven, of that profane nation,
49And gently report thy next transmigration.

ANDROGYNO

50To the same that I am.

NANO

To the same that I am. A creature of delight,
51And, what is more than a fool, an hermaphrodite!
52Now, prithee, sweet soul, in all thy variation,
53Which body would’st thou choose, to keep up thy station?

ANDROGYNO

54Troth, this I am in: even here would I tarry.

NANO

55'Cause here the delight of each sex thou canst vary?

ANDROGYNO

56Alas, those pleasures be stale and forsaken;
57No, 'tis your fool wherewith I am so taken,
58The only one creature that I can call blessed;
59For all other forms I have proved most distressed.

NANO

60Spoke true, as thou wert in Pythagoras still.
61This learned opinion we celebrate will,
62Fellow eunuch, as behoves us, with all our wit and art,
63To dignify that whereof ourselves are so great and
64special a part.

VOLPONE

65Now, very, very pretty! Mosca, this
66Was thy invention?

MOSCA

Was thy invention? If it please my patron,
67Not else.

VOLPONE

Not else. It doth, good Mosca.

MOSCA

Not else. It doth, good Mosca. Then it was, sir.

[song]

68Fools, they are the only nation
69Worth men's envy or admiration:
70Free from care or sorrow-taking,
71Selves and others merry making:
72All they speak or do is sterling.
73Your fool he is your great man's darling,
74And your ladies’ sport and pleasure;
75Tongue and bauble are his treasure.
76E'en his face begetteth laughter,
77And he speaks truth free from slaughter;
78He's the grace of every feast,
79And sometimes the chiefest guest;
80Hath his trencher and his stool,
81When wit waits upon the fool.
82O, who would not be
83He, he, he?

One knocks without.

VOLPONE

84Who's that? Away!
85[Exeunt Nano and Castrone.] Look, Mosca.

[Exit Androgyno.]

MOSCA

[Exeunt Nano and Castrone.] Look, Mosca. Fool begone!
86'Tis Signor Voltore, the advocate;
87I know him by his knock.

VOLPONE

I know him by his knock. Fetch me my gown,
88My furs and night-caps; say, my couch is changing,
89And let him entertain himself awhile
90Without i' the gallery.
Without i' the gallery. [Exit Mosca.] Now, now, my clients
91Begin their visitation! Vulture, kite,
92Raven, and gor-crow, all my birds of prey,
93That think me turning carcass, now they come;
94I am not for them yet-
I am not for them yet- [Re-enter Mosca, with the gown, etc.] How now! The news?

MOSCA

95A piece of plate, sir.

VOLPONE

A piece of plate, sir. Of what bigness?

MOSCA

A piece of plate, sir. Of what bigness? Huge,
96Massy, and antique, with your name inscribed,
97And arms engraven.

VOLPONE

And arms engraven. Good! And not a fox
98Streched on the earth, with fine delusive sleights,
99Mocking a gaping crow? ha, Mosca!

MOSCA

Mocking a gaping crow? ha, Mosca! Sharp, sir.

VOLPONE

100Give me my furs. Why dost thou laugh so, man?

MOSCA

101I cannot choose, sir, when I apprehend
102What thoughts he has without now, as he walks:
103That this might be the last gift he should give;
104That this would fetch you; if you died to-day,
105And gave him all, what he should be to-morrow;
106What large return would come of all his ventures;
107How he should worshiped be, and reverenced;
108Ride with his furs, and foot-cloths; waited on
109By herds of fools, and clients; have clear way
110Made for his mule, as lettered as himself;
111Be called the great and learned advocate:
112And then concludes, there's naught impossible.

VOLPONE

113Yes, to be learned, Mosca.

MOSCA

Yes, to be learned, Mosca. O, no: rich
114Implies it. Hood an ass with reverend purple,
115So you can hide his two ambitious ears,
116And he shall pass for a cathedral doctor.

VOLPONE

117My caps, my caps, good Mosca. Fetch him in.

MOSCA

118Stay, sir; your ointment for your eyes.

VOLPONE

Stay, sir; your ointment for your eyes. That's true;
119Dispatch, dispatch: I long to have possession
120Of my new present.

MOSCA

Of my new present. That, and thousands more,
121I hope to see you lord of.

VOLPONE

I hope to see you lord of. Thanks, kind Mosca.

MOSCA

122And that, when I am lost in blended dust,
123And hundred such as I am, in succession -

VOLPONE

124Nay, that were too much, Mosca.

MOSCA

Nay, that were too much, Mosca. You shall live
125Still, to delude these harpies.

VOLPONE

Still, to delude these harpies. Loving Mosca!
126'Tis well: my pillow now, and let him enter.
127[Exit Mosca.] Now, my feigned cough, my phthisic, and my gout,
128My apoplexy, palsy, and catarrhs,
129Help, with your forced functions, this my posture,
130Wherein, this three year, I have milked their hopes.
131He comes; I hear him-Uh!
He comes; I hear him-Uh! [Coughing.] uh, uh, uh, uh! O -

ACT 1, Scene 3

[Enter Mosca, ushering in Voltore, carrying a platter.]

MOSCA

1You still are what you were, sir. Only you,
2Of all the rest, are he commands his love,
3And you do wisely to preserve it thus,
4With early visitation, and kind notes
5Of your good meaning to him, which, I know,
6Cannot but come most grateful. Patron! Sir!
7Here's Signior Voltore is come-

VOLPONE

Here's Signior Voltore is come- [Faintly.] What say you?

MOSCA

8Sir, Signior Voltore is come this morning
9To visit you.

VOLPONE

To visit you. I thank him.

MOSCA

To visit you. I thank him. And hath brought
10A piece of antique plate, bought of St. Mark,
11With which he here presents you.

VOLPONE

With which he here presents you. He is welcome.
12Pray him to come more often.

MOSCA

Pray him to come more often. Yes.

VOLTORE

Pray him to come more often. Yes. What says he?

MOSCA

13He thanks you, and desires you see him often.

VOLPONE

14Mosca.

MOSCA

Mosca. My patron!

VOLPONE

Mosca. My patron! Bring him near, where is he?
15I long to feel his hand.

MOSCA

I long to feel his hand. The plate is here, sir.

VOLTORE

16How fare you, sir?

VOLPONE

How fare you, sir? I thank you, Signor Voltore;
17Where is the plate? Mine eyes are bad.

VOLTORE

Where is the plate? Mine eyes are bad. [Putting it into his hands.] I'm sorry,
18To see you still thus weak.

MOSCA

To see you still thus weak. [aside] That he’s not weaker.aparte

VOLPONE

19[Taking hold of the platter.] You are too munificent.

VOLTORE

[Taking hold of the platter.] You are too munificent. No, sir; would to heaven,
20I could as well give health to you, as that plate!

VOLPONE

21You give, sir, what you can: I thank you. Your love
22Hath taste in this, and shall not be unanswered:
23I pray you see me often.

VOLTORE

I pray you see me often. Yes, I shall, sir.

VOLPONE

24Be not far from me.

MOSCA

Be not far from me. [To Voltore] Do you observe that, sir?aparte

VOLPONE

25Hearken unto me still; it will concern you.

MOSCA

26[To Voltore] You are a happy man, sir; know your good.aparte

VOLPONE

27I cannot now last long -

MOSCA

I cannot now last long - [To Voltore] You are his heir, sir.aparte

VOLTORE

28Am I?

VOLPONE

29I feel me going; uh! uh! uh! uh!
30I’m sailing to my port, uh! uh! uh! uh!
31And I am glad I am so near my haven.

MOSCA

32Alas, kind gentleman! Well, we must all go -

VOLTORE

33But, Mosca -

MOSCA

But, Mosca - Age will conquer.

VOLTORE

But, Mosca - Age will conquer. Pray thee, hear me:
34Am I inscribed his heir for certain?

MOSCA

Am I inscribed his heir for certain? Are you!
35I do beseech you, sir, you will vouchsafe
36To write me in your family. All my hopes
37Depend upon your worship: I am lost,
38Except the rising sun do shine on me.

VOLTORE

39It shall both shine, and warm thee, Mosca.

MOSCA

40Sir,
41I am a man, that hath not done your love
42All the worst offices: here I wear your keys,
43See all your coffers and your caskets locked,
44Keep the poor inventory of your jewels,
45Your plate and monies; am your steward, sir,
46Husband your goods here.

VOLTORE

Husband your goods here. But am I sole heir?

MOSCA

47Without a partner, sir; confirmed this morning:
48The wax is warm yet, and the ink scarce dry
49Upon the parchment.

VOLTORE

Upon the parchment. Happy, happy, me!
50By what good chance, sweet Mosca?

MOSCA

By what good chance, sweet Mosca? Your desert, sir;
51I know no second cause.

VOLTORE

I know no second cause. Thy modesty
52Is not to know it; well, we shall requite it.

MOSCA

53He ever liked your course, sir; that first took him.
54I oft have heard him say, how he admired
55Men of your large profession, that could speak
56To every cause, and things mere contraries,
57Till they were hoarse again, yet all be law;
58That, with most quick agility, could turn,
59And return; make knots, and undo them;
60Give forked counsel; take provoking gold
61On either hand, and put it up: these men,
62He knew, would thrive with their humility.
63And, for his part, he thought he should be blest
64To have his heir of such a suffering spirit,
65So wise, so grave, of so perplexed a tongue,
66And loud withal, that would not wag, nor scarce
67Lie still, without a fee, when every word
68Your worship but lets fall, is a cecchine!
69(Another knocks.) Who's that? one knocks; I would not have you seen, sir.
70And yet — pretend you came, and went in haste:
71I'll fashion an excuse — and, gentle sir,
72When you do come to swim in golden lard,
73Up to the arms in honey, that your chin
74Is borne up stiff, with fatness of the flood,
75Think on your vassal; but remember me:
76I have not been your worst of clients.

VOLTORE

I have not been your worst of clients. Mosca!—

MOSCA

77When will you have your inventory brought, sir?
78Or see a copy of the will? —Anon! —
79I'll bring them to you, sir. Away, be gone,
80Put business in your face.

[Exit Voltore.]

VOLPONE

Put business in your face. [Springing up.] Excellent, Mosca!
81Come hither, let me kiss thee.

MOSCA

Come hither, let me kiss thee. Keep you still, sir.
82Here is Corbaccio.

VOLPONE

Here is Corbaccio. Set the plate away:
83The vulture's gone, and the old raven's come!

ACT 1, Scene 4

MOSCA

1Betake you to your silence, and your sleep.
2[Putting the plate aside.] Stand there and multiply. Now, we shall see
3A wretch who is indeed more impotent
4Than this can feign to be; yet hopes to hop
5Over his grave-
Over his grave- [Enter Corbaccio.] Signior Corbaccio!
6You're very welcome, sir.

CORBACCIO

You're very welcome, sir. How does your patron?

MOSCA

7Troth, as he did, sir; no amends.

CORBACCIO

Troth, as he did, sir; no amends. What! mends he?

MOSCA

8No, sir: he’s rather worse.

CORBACCIO

No, sir: he’s rather worse. That's well. Where is he?

MOSCA

9Upon his couch, sir, newly fallen asleep.

CORBACCIO

10Does he sleep well?

MOSCA

Does he sleep well? No wink, sir, all this night.
11Nor yesterday; but slumbers.

CORBACCIO

Nor yesterday; but slumbers. Good! He should take
12Some counsel of physicians: I have brought him
13An opiate here, from mine own doctor.

MOSCA

14He will not hear of drugs.

CORBACCIO

He will not hear of drugs. Why? I myself
15Stood by while it was made, saw all the ingredients:
16And know, it cannot but most gently work:
17My life for his, 'tis but to make him sleep.

VOLPONE

18[Aside] Aye, his last sleep, if he would take it.aparte

MOSCA

19Sir,
Sir, He has no faith in physic.

CORBACCIO

Sir, He has no faith in physic. Say you, say you?

MOSCA

20He has no faith in physic: he does think
21Most of your doctors are the greater danger
22And worse disease, to escape. I often have
23Heard him protest, that your physician
24Should never be his heir.

CORBACCIO

Should never be his heir. Not I his heir?

MOSCA

25Not your physician, sir.

CORBACCIO

Not your physician, sir. O, no, no, no,
26I do not mean it.

MOSCA

I do not mean it. No, sir, nor their fees
27He cannot brook: he says, they flay a man,
28Before they kill him.

CORBACCIO

Before they kill him. Right, I do conceive you.

MOSCA

29And then they do it by experiment;
30For which the law not only doth absolve them,
31But gives them great reward: and he is loath
32To hire his death, so.

CORBACCIO

To hire his death, so. It is true, they kill
33With as much license as a judge.

MOSCA

With as much license as a judge. Nay, more;
34For he but kills, sir, where the law condemns,
35And these can kill him too.

CORBACCIO

And these can kill him too. Aye, or me;
36Or any man. How does his apoplex?
37Is that strong on him still?

MOSCA

Is that strong on him still? Most violent.
38His speech is broken, and his eyes are set,
39His face drawn longer than 'twas wont–

CORBACCIO

His face drawn longer than 'twas wont– How! how!
40Stronger than he was wont?

MOSCA

Stronger than he was wont? No, sir: his face
41Drawn longer than 'twas wont.

CORBACCIO

Drawn longer than 'twas wont. O, good!

MOSCA

Drawn longer than 'twas wont. O, good! His mouth
42Is ever gaping, and his eyelids hang.

CORBACCIO

Is ever gaping, and his eyelids hang. Good.

MOSCA

43A freezing numbness stiffens all his joints,
44And makes the colour of his flesh like lead.

CORBACCIO

And makes the colour of his flesh like lead. ‘Tis good.

MOSCA

45His pulse beats slow, and dull.

CORBACCIO

His pulse beats slow, and dull. Good symptoms still.

MOSCA

46And from his brain–

CORBACCIO

And from his brain– Ha? How? not from his brain?

MOSCA

47Yes, sir, and from his brain–

CORBACCIO

Yes, sir, and from his brain– I conceive you; good.

MOSCA

48Flows a cold sweat, with a continual rheum,
49Forth the resolved corners of his eyes.

CORBACCIO

50Is't possible? Yet I am better, ha!
51How does he, with the swimming of his head?

MOSCA

52O, sir, 'tis past the scotomy; he now
53Hath lost his feeling, and hath left to snort:
54Your hardly can perceive him, that he breathes.

CORBACCIO

55Excellent, excellent! sure I shall outlast him:
56This makes me young again, a score of years.

MOSCA

57I was a coming for you, sir.

CORBACCIO

I was a coming for you, sir. Has he made his will?
58What has he given me?

MOSCA

What has he given me? No, sir.

CORBACCIO

What has he given me? No, sir. Nothing! Ha?

MOSCA

59He has not made his will, sir.

CORBACCIO

He has not made his will, sir. Oh, oh, oh!
60What then did Voltore, the lawyer, here?

MOSCA

61He smelt a carcass, sir, when he but heard
62My master was about his testament;
63As I did urge him to it for your good -

CORBACCIO

64He came unto him, did he? I thought so.

MOSCA

65Yes, and presented him this piece of plate.

CORBACCIO

66To be his heir?

MOSCA

To be his heir? I do not know, sir.

CORBACCIO

To be his heir? I do not know, sir. True:
67I know it too.

MOSCA

I know it too. [aside.] By your own scale, sir.aparte

CORBACCIO

I know it too. [aside.] By your own scale, sir. Well,
68I shall prevent him, yet. See, Mosca, look,
69Here, I have brought a bag of bright cecchines,
70Will quite weigh down his plate.

MOSCA

Will quite weigh down his plate. [Taking the bag.] Yea, marry, sir.
71This is true physic, this your sacred medicine;
72No talk of opiates, to this great elixir!

CORBACCIO

73'Tis aurum palpabile, if not potabile.

MOSCA

74It shall be ministered to him, in his bowl.

CORBACCIO

75Ay, do, do, do.

MOSCA

Ay, do, do, do. Most blessed cordial!
76This will recover him.

CORBACCIO

This will recover him. Yes, do, do, do.

MOSCA

77I think it were not best, sir.

CORBACCIO

I think it were not best, sir. What?

MOSCA

I think it were not best, sir. What? To recover him.

CORBACCIO

78O, no, no, no; by no means.

MOSCA

O, no, no, no; by no means. Why, sir, this
79Will work some strange effect, if he but feel it.

CORBACCIO

80'Tis true, therefore forbear, I'll take my venture:
81Give me it again.

MOSCA

Give me it again. At no hand; pardon me:
82You shall not do yourself that wrong, sir. I
83Will so advise you, you shall have it all.

CORBACCIO

84How?

MOSCA

How? All, sir; 'tis your right, your own: no man
85Can claim a part: 'tis yours, without a rival,
86Decreed by destiny.

CORBACCIO

Decreed by destiny. How, how, good Mosca?

MOSCA

87I'll tell you, sir. This fit he shall recover.

CORBACCIO

88I do conceive you.

MOSCA

I do conceive you. And, on first advantage
89Of his gained sense, will I re-importune him
90Unto the making of his testament:
91And show him this.

[Pointing to the money.]

CORBACCIO

And show him this. Good, good.

MOSCA

And show him this. Good, good. 'Tis better yet,
92If you will hear, sir.

CORBACCIO

If you will hear, sir. Yes, with all my heart.

MOSCA

93Now, would I counsel you, make home with speed;
94There, frame a will; whereto you shall inscribe
95My master your sole heir.

CORBACCIO

My master your sole heir. And disinherit
96My son!

MOSCA

My son! O, sir, the better: for that colour
97Shall make it much more taking.

CORBACCIO

Shall make it much more taking. O, but colour?

MOSCA

98This will, sir, you shall send it unto me.
99Now, when I come to enforce, as I will do,
100Your cares, your watchings, and your many prayers,
101Your more than many gifts, your this day’s present,
102And last, produce your will; where, without thought,
103Or least regard, unto your proper issue,
104A son so brave, and highly meriting,
105The stream of your diverted love hath thrown you
106Upon my master, and made him your heir:
107He cannot be so stupid, or stone-dead,
108But out of conscience, and mere gratitude–

CORBACCIO

109He must pronounce me his?

MOSCA

He must pronounce me his? ‘Tis true.

CORBACCIO

He must pronounce me his? ‘Tis true. This plot
110Did I think on before.

MOSCA

Did I think on before. I do believe it.

CORBACCIO

111Do you not believe it?

MOSCA

Do you not believe it? Yes, sir.

CORBACCIO

Do you not believe it? Yes, sir. Mine own project.

MOSCA

112Which, when he hath done, sir–

CORBACCIO

Which, when he hath done, sir– Published me his heir?

MOSCA

113And you so certain to survive him–

CORBACCIO

And you so certain to survive him– Aye.

MOSCA

114Being so lusty a man–

CORBACCIO

Being so lusty a man– ‘Tis true.

MOSCA

Being so lusty a man– ‘Tis true. Yes, sir–

CORBACCIO

115I thought on that too. See, how he should be
116The very organ to express my thoughts!

MOSCA

117You have not only done yourself a good–

CORBACCIO

118But multiplied it on my son.

MOSCA

But multiplied it on my son. ‘Tis right, sir.

CORBACCIO

119Still, my invention.

MOSCA

Still, my invention. ‘Las, sir! heaven knows,
120It hath been all my study, all my care,
121(I e’en grow gray withal), how to work things–

CORBACCIO

122I do conceive, sweet Mosca.

MOSCA

I do conceive, sweet Mosca. You are he,
123For whom I labour here.

CORBACCIO

For whom I labour here. Ay, do, do, do:
124I’ll straight about it.

[Going.]

MOSCA

I’ll straight about it. [Aside] Rook go with you, raven!aparte

CORBACCIO

125I know thee honest.

MOSCA

I know thee honest. You do lie, sir!

CORBACCIO

I know thee honest. You do lie, sir! And –

MOSCA

126Your knowledge is no better than your ears, sir.

CORBACCIO

127I do not doubt, to be a father to thee.

MOSCA

128Nor I to gull my brother of his blessing.

CORBACCIO

129I may have my youth restored to me, why not?

MOSCA

130Your worship is a precious ass!

CORBACCIO

Your worship is a precious ass! What say’st thou?

MOSCA

131I do desire your worship to make haste, sir.

CORBACCIO

132‘Tis done. ‘tis done; I go.

[Exit.]

VOLPONE

‘Tis done. ‘tis done; I go. [Leaping up.] Oh, I shall burst!
133Let out my sides, let out my sides –

MOSCA

Let out my sides, let out my sides – Contain
134Your flux of laughter, sir: you know this hope
135Is such a bait, it covers any hook.

VOLPONE

136Oh, but thy working, and thy placing it!
137I cannot hold; good rascal, let me kiss thee:
138I never knew thee in so rare a humour.

MOSCA

139Alas, sir, I but do as I am taught;
140Follow your grave instructions; give them words;
141Pour oil into their ears, and send them hence.

VOLPONE

142‘Tis true, ‘tis true. What a rare punishment
143Is avarice to itself!

MOSCA

Is avarice to itself! Aye, with our help, sir.

VOLPONE

144So many cares, so many maladies,
145So many fears attending on old age,
146Yea, death so often called on, as no wish
147Can be more frequent with them, their limbs faint,
148Their senses dull, their seeing, hearing, going,
149All dead before them; yea, their very teeth,
150Their instruments of eating, failing them:
151Yet this is reckoned life! nay, here was one,
152Is now gone home, that wishes to live longer!
153Feels not his gout, nor palsy; feigns himself
154Younger by scores of years, flatters his age
155With confident belying it, hopes he may,
156With charms, like Aeson, have his youth restored:
157And with these thoughts so battens, as if fate
158Would be as easily cheated on, as he,
159And all turns air!
And all turns air! (Another knocks.) Who’s that there, now? A third!

MOSCA

160Close, to your couch again; I hear his voice:
161It is Corvino, our spruce merchant.

VOLPONE

It is Corvino, our spruce merchant. Dead.

MOSCA

162Another bout, sir, with your eyes. Who’s there?

ACT 1, Scene 5

[Enter Corvino.]

MOSCA

1Signior Corvino! Come most wished for! O,
2How happy were you, if you knew it, now!

CORVINO

3Why? what? wherein?

MOSCA

Why? what? wherein? The tardy hour is come, sir.

CORVINO

4He is not dead?

MOSCA

He is not dead? Not dead, sir, but as good;
5He knows no man.

CORVINO

He knows no man. How shall I do, then?

MOSCA

He knows no man. How shall I do, then? Why, sir?

CORVINO

6I have brought him here a pearl.

MOSCA

I have brought him here a pearl. Perhaps he has
7So much remembrance left, as to know you, sir:
8He still calls on you; nothing but your name
9Is in his mouth. Is your pearl orient, sir?

CORVINO

10Venice was never owner of the like.

VOLPONE

11[Faintly.] Signior Corvino!

MOSCA

[Faintly.] Signior Corvino! Hark.

VOLPONE

[Faintly.] Signior Corvino! Hark. Signior Corvino!

MOSCA

12He calls you; step and give it him. – He’s here, sir,
13And he has brought you a rich pearl.

CORVINO

And he has brought you a rich pearl. [to Voltone] How do you, sir?
14[To Mosca] Tell him, it doubles the twelfth carat.

MOSCA

[To Mosca] Tell him, it doubles the twelfth carat. Sir,
15He cannot understand, his hearing’s gone;
16And yet it comforts him to see you –

CORVINO

And yet it comforts him to see you – Say,
17I have a diamond for him, too.

MOSCA

I have a diamond for him, too. Best show it, sir;
18Put it into his hand; ‘tis only there
19He apprehends: he has his feeling, yet.
20See how he grasps it!

CORVINO

See how he grasps it! ‘Las, good gentleman!
21How pitiful the sight is!

MOSCA

How pitiful the sight is! Tut! forget, sir.
22The weeping of an heir should still be laughter
23Under a visor.

CORVINO

Under a visor. Why, am I his heir?

MOSCA

24Sir, I am sworn, I may not show the will
25Till he be dead; But here has been Corbaccio,
26Here has been Voltore, here were others too,
27I cannot number ‘em, they were so many;
28All gaping here for legacies: but I,
29Taking the vantage of his naming you,
30“Signior Corvino! Signior Corvino!”, took
31Paper, and pen, and ink, and there I asked him,
32Whom he would have his heir. “Corvino.” Who
33Should be executor? “Corvino.” And,
34To any question he was silent to,
35I still interpreted the nods he made,
36Through weakness, for consent: and sent home th’others,
37Nothing bequeathed them, but to cry and curse.

[They embrace.]

CORVINO

38O, my dear Mosca! Does he not perceive us?

MOSCA

39No more than a blind harper. He knows no man,
40No face of friend, nor name of any servant,
41Who ‘twas that fed him last, or gave him drink:
42Not those he hath begotten, or brought up,
43Can he remember.

CORVINO

Can he remember. Has he children?

MOSCA

Can he remember. Has he children? Bastards,
44Some dozen, or more, that he begot on beggars,
45Gypsies, and Jews, and black-moors, when he was drunk.
46Knew you not that, sir? ‘tis the common fable.
47The dwarf, the fool, the eunuch, are all his;
48He’s the true father of his family,
49In all, save me:- but he has given them nothing.

CORVINO

50That’s well, that’s well! Art sure he does not hear us?

MOSCA

51Sure, sir! why, look you, credit your own sense.
52[Shouts in Volpone’s ear] The pox approach, and add to your diseases,
53If it would send you hence the sooner, sir.
54For your incontinence, it hath deserved it
55Throughly, and throughly, and the plague to boot!—
56You may come near, sir. —Would you would once close
57Those filthy eyes of yours, that flow with slime,
58Like two frog-pits; and those same hanging cheeks,
59Covered with hide instead of skin – Nay, help, sir –
60That look like frozen dish-clouts set on end!

CORVINO

61Or like an old smoked wall, on which the rain
62Ran down in streaks!

MOSCA

Ran down in streaks! Excellent, sir! speak out:
63You may be louder yet; a culverin
64Discharged in his ear would hardly bore it.

CORVINO

65His nose is like a common sewer, still running.

MOSCA

66‘Tis good! And what his mouth?

CORVINO

‘Tis good! And what his mouth? A very draught.

MOSCA

67O, stop it up –

CORVINO

O, stop it up – By no means.

MOSCA

O, stop it up – By no means. ‘Pray you, let me:
68Faith, I could stifle him rarely with a pillow.
69As well as any woman that should keep him.

CORVINO

70Do you as will; but I’ll be gone.

MOSCA

Do you as will; but I’ll be gone. Be so:
71It is your presence makes him last so long.

CORVINO

72I pray you, use no violence.

MOSCA

I pray you, use no violence. No, sir? Why?
73Why should you be thus scrupulous, pray you, sir?

CORVINO

74Nay, at your discretion.

MOSCA

Nay, at your discretion. Well, good sir, begone.

CORVINO

75I will not trouble him now, to take my pearl.

MOSCA

76Puh! nor your diamond. What a needless care
77Is this afflicts you? Is not all here yours?
78Am not I here, whom you have made your creature?
79That owe my being to you?

CORVINO

That owe my being to you? Grateful Mosca!
80Thou art my friend, my fellow, my companion,
81My partner, and shalt share in all my fortunes.

MOSCA

82Excepting one.

CORVINO

Excepting one. What’s that?

MOSCA

Excepting one. What’s that? Your gallant wife, sir.-
83[Exit Corvino.] Now is he gone: we had no other means
84To shoot him hence, but this.

VOLPONE

To shoot him hence, but this. My divine Mosca!
85Thou hast to-day outgone thyself.
Thou hast to-day outgone thyself. (Another knocks.) Who’s there?
86I will be troubled with no more. Prepare
87Me music, dances, banquets, all delights;
88The Turk is not more sensual in his pleasures,
89Than will Volpone
Than will Volpone [Exit Mosca.] Let me see; a pearl!
90A diamond! Plate! Cecchines! Good morning’s purchase.
91Why, this is better than rob churches, yet;
92Or fat, by eating, once a month, a man—
93[Re-enter Mosca.] Who is’t?

MOSCA

[Re-enter Mosca.] Who is’t? The beauteous Lady Would-be, sir,
94Wife to the English knight, Sir Politic Would-be,
95(This is the style, sir, is directed me,)
96Hath sent to know how you have slept to-night,
97And if you would be visited?

VOLPONE

And if you would be visited? Not now:
98Some three hours hence –

MOSCA

Some three hours hence – I told the squire so much.

VOLPONE

99When I am high with mirth and wine; then, then:
100‘Fore heaven, I wonder at the desperate valor
101Of the bold English, that they dare let loose
102Their wives to all encounters!

MOSCA

Their wives to all encounters! Sir, this knight
103Had not his name for nothing, he is politic,
104And knows, howe’er his wife affect strange airs,
105She hath not yet the face to be dishonest:
106But had she Signior Corvino’s wife’s face –

VOLPONE

107Has she so rare a face?

MOSCA

Has she so rare a face? O, sir, the wonder,
108The blazing star of Italy! a wench
109Of the first year! a beauty ripe as harvest!
110Whose skin is whiter than a swan all over,
111Than silver, snow, or lilies! a soft lip,
112Would tempt you to eternity of kissing!
113And flesh that melteth in the touch to blood!
114Bright as your gold, and lovely as your gold!

VOLPONE

115Why had not I known this before?

MOSCA

Why had not I known this before? Alas, sir,
116Myself but yesterday discovered it.

VOLPONE

117How might I see her?

MOSCA

How might I see her? O, not possible;
118She’s kept as warily as is your gold;
119Never does come abroad, never takes air,
120But at a window. All her looks are sweet,
121As the first grapes or cherries, and are watched
122As near as they are.

VOLPONE

As near as they are. I must see her.

MOSCA

As near as they are. I must see her. Sir,
123There is a guard of spies ten thick upon her,
124All his whole household; each of which is set
125Upon his fellow, and have all their charge,
126When he goes out, when he comes in, examined.

VOLPONE

127I will go see her, though but at her window.

MOSCA

128In some disguise, then.

VOLPONE

In some disguise, then. That is true; I must
129Maintain mine own shape still the same: we’ll think.

[Exeunt.]

ACT 2

SCENE 1

[Enter Politic Would-be, Peregrine]

SIR POLITIC

1Sir, to a wise man, all the world’s his soil:
2It is not Italy, nor France, nor Europe,
3That must bound me, if my fates call me forth.
4Yet, I protest, it is no salt desire
5Of seeing countries, shifting a religion,
6Nor any disaffection to the state
7Where I was bred, and unto which I owe
8My dearest plots, hath brought me out; much less,
9That idle, antique, stale, gray-headed project
10Of knowing men’s minds and manners, with Ulysses!
11But a peculiar humor of my wife’s
12Laid for this height of Venice, to observe,
13To quote, to learn the language, and so forth –
14I hope you travel, sir, with license?

PEREGRINE

I hope you travel, sir, with license? Yes.

SIR POLITIC

15I dare the safelier converse- How long, sir,
16Since you left England?

PEREGRINE

Since you left England? Seven weeks.

SIR POLITIC

Since you left England? Seven weeks. So lately!
17You have not been with my Lord Ambassador?

PEREGRINE

You have not been with my Lord Ambassador? Not yet, sir.

SIR POLITIC

18Pray you, what news, sir, vents our Climate?
19I heard last night a most strange thing reported
20By some of my lord’s followers, and I long
21To hear how ‘twill be seconded.

PEREGRINE

To hear how ‘twill be seconded. What was’t, sir?

SIR POLITIC

22Marry, sir, of a raven that should build
23In a ship royal of the king’s.

PEREGRINE

In a ship royal of the king’s. [Aside.] This fellow,aparte
24Does he gull me, trow? or is gulled? – Your name, sir?

SIR POLITIC

25My name is Politic Would-be,

PEREGRINE

My name is Politic Would-be, [Aside] O, that speaks him –aparte
26A knight, sir?

SIR POLITIC

A knight, sir? A poor knight, sir.

PEREGRINE

A knight, sir? A poor knight, sir. Your lady
27Lies here in Venice, for intelligence
28Of tires, and fashions, and behaviour,
29Among the courtesans? The fine Lady Would-be?

SIR POLITIC

30Yes, sir; the spider and the bee, oft times,
31Suck from one flower.

PEREGRINE

Suck from one flower. Good Sir Politic,
32I cry you mercy; I have heard much of you:
33‘Tis true, sir, of your raven.

SIR POLITIC

‘Tis true, sir, of your raven. On your knowledge?

PEREGRINE

34Yes, and your lion’s whelping in the Tower.

SIR POLITIC

35Another whelp!

PEREGRINE

Another whelp! Another, sir.

SIR POLITIC

Another whelp! Another, sir. Now, heaven!
36What prodigies be these? The fires at Berwick!
37And the new star! These things concurring, strange,
38And full of omen! Saw you those meteors?

PEREGRINE

39I did, sir.

SIR POLITIC

I did, sir. Fearful! Pray you, sir, confirm me,
40Were there three porpoises seen above the Bridge,
41As they give out?

PEREGRINE

As they give out? Six, and a sturgeon, sir.

SIR POLITIC

42I am astonished.

PEREGRINE

I am astonished. Nay, sir, be not so;
43I’ll tell you a greater prodigy than these.

SIR POLITIC

44What should these things portend?

PEREGRINE

What should these things portend? The very day
45(Let me be sure) that I put forth from London,
46There was a whale discovered in the river,
47As high as Woolwich, that had waited there,
48Few know how many months, for the subversion
49Of the Stode Fleet.

SIR POLITIC

Of the Stode Fleet. Is’t possible? believe it,
50‘Twas either sent from Spain, or the archdukes:
51Spinola’s whale, upon my life, my credit!
52Will they not leave these projects? Worthy sir,
53Some other news.

PEREGRINE

Some other news. Faith, Stone the fool is dead,
54And they do lack a tavern fool extremely.

SIR POLITIC

55Is Mas’ Stone dead?

PEREGRINE

Is Mas’ Stone dead? He’s dead, sir; why, I hope
56You thought him not immortal?
You thought him not immortal? [Aside] O, this knight,aparte
57Were he well known, would be a precious thing
58To fit our English stage: he that should write
59But such a fellow, should be thought to feign
60Extremely, if not maliciously.

SIR POLITIC

Extremely, if not maliciously. Stone dead!

PEREGRINE

61Dead.— Lord! how deeply, sir, you apprehend it?
62He was no kinsman to you?

SIR POLITIC

He was no kinsman to you? That I know of.
63Well! that same fellow was an unknown fool.

PEREGRINE

64And yet you knew him, it seems?

SIR POLITIC

And yet you knew him, it seems? I did so. Sir,
65I knew him one of the most dangerous heads
66Living within the state, and so I held him.

PEREGRINE

67Indeed, sir?

SIR POLITIC

Indeed, sir? While he lived, in action,
68He has received weekly intelligence,
69Upon my knowledge, out of the Low Countries,
70For all parts of the world, in cabbages;
71And those dispensed again to ambassadors
72In oranges, musk-melons, apricots,
73Lemons, pome-citrons, and such-like; sometimes
74In Colchester oysters, and your Selsey cockles.

PEREGRINE

75You make me wonder.

SIR POLITIC

You make me wonder. Sir, upon my knowledge.
76Nay, I’ve observed him, at your public ordinary,
77Take his advertisement from a traveller,
78A concealed statesman, in a trencher of meat;
79And instantly, before the meal was done,
80Convey an answer in a tooth-pick.

PEREGRINE

Convey an answer in a tooth-pick. Strange!
81How could this be, sir?

SIR POLITIC

How could this be, sir? Why, the meat was cut
82so like his character, and so laid, as he
83must easily read the cipher.

PEREGRINE

must easily read the cipher. I have heard,
84He could not read, sir.

SIR POLITIC

He could not read, sir. So ‘twas given out,
85In policy, by those that did employ him:
86But he could read, and had your languages,
87And to’t, as sound a noddle –

PEREGRINE

And to’t, as sound a noddle – I have heard, sir,
88That your baboons were spies, and that they were
89A kind of subtle nation near to China.

SIR POLITIC

90Aye, aye, your Mamuluchi. Faith, they had
91Their hand in a French plot or two; but they
92Were so extremely given to women, as
93They made discovery of all: yet I
94Had my advices here, on Wednesday last.
95From one of their own coat, they were returned,
96Made their relations, as the fashion is,
97And now stand fair for fresh employment.

PEREGRINE

And now stand fair for fresh employment. [Aside] ’Heart!aparte
98This Sir Pol will be ignorant of nothing.
99It seems, sir, you know all.

SIR POLITIC

It seems, sir, you know all. Not all, sir, but
100I have some general notions. I do love
101To note and to observe: though I live out,
102Free from the active torrent, yet I’d mark
103The currents and the passages of things,
104For mine own private use; and know the ebbs
105And flows of state.

PEREGRINE

And flows of state. Believe it, sir, I hold
106Myself in no small tie unto my fortunes,
107For casting me thus luckily upon you,
108Whose knowledge, if your bounty equal it,
109May do me great assistance, in instruction
110For my behaviour, and my bearing, which
111Is yet so rude and raw.

SIR POLITIC

Is yet so rude and raw. Why, came you forth
112Empty of rules for travel?

PEREGRINE

Empty of rules for travel? Faith, I had
113Some common ones, from out that vulgar grammar,
114Which he that cried Italian to me, taught me.

SIR POLITIC

115Why this it is that spoils all our brave bloods,
116Trusting our hopeful gentry unto pedants.
117Fellows of outside, and mere bark. You seem
118To be a gentleman, of ingenuous race: —
119I not profess it, but my fate hath been
120To be, where I have been consulted with,
121In this high kind, touching some great men’s sons,
122Persons of blood and honour. –

PEREGRINE

Persons of blood and honour. – Who be these, sir?

ACT 1, SCENE 2

(Enter Mosca, Nano followed by Grege.)

MOSCA

1Under that window, there it must be. The same.

[They set out a platform.]

SIR POLITIC

2Fellows, to mount a bank. Did your instructor
3In the dear tongues, never discourse to you
4Of the Italian mountebanks?

PEREGRINE

Of the Italian mountebanks? Yes, sir.

SIR POLITIC

Of the Italian mountebanks? Yes, sir. Why,
5Here you shall see one.

PEREGRINE

Here you shall see one. They are quacksalvers;
6Fellows, that live by venting oils and drugs.

SIR POLITIC

7Was that the character he gave you of them?

PEREGRINE

8As I remember.

SIR POLITIC

As I remember. Pity his ignorance.
9They are the only knowing men of Europe!
10Great general scholars, excellent physicians,
11Most admired statesmen, professed favourites,
12And cabinet counsellors to the greatest princes;
13The only languaged men of all the world!

PEREGRINE

14And I have heard, they are most lewd impostors;
15Made all of terms and shreds; no less beliers
16Of great men’s favours, than their own vile med’cines;
17Which they will utter upon monstrous oaths:
18Selling that drug for two-pence, ere they part,
19Which they have valued at twelve crowns before.

SIR POLITIC

20Sir, calumnies are answered best with silence.
21Yourself shall judge. — Who is it mounts, my friends?

MOSCA

22Scoto of Mantua, sir.

SIR POLITIC

Scoto of Mantua, sir. Is’t he? Nay, then
23I’ll proudly promise, sir, you shall behold
24Another man than has been phant’sied to you.
25I wonder yet, that he should mount his bank,
26Here in this nook, that has been wont t’appear
27In face of the piazza!—Here he comes.

[Enter Volpone, disguised as a mountebank doctor, and followed by a crowd of people.]

VOLPONE

28[To Nano] Mount, zany.

GREGE

[To Nano] Mount, zany. Follow, follow, follow, follow, follow!

SIR POLITIC

29See how the people follow him! He’s a man
30May write ten thousand crowns in bank here. Note,
31[Volpone mounts the platform.] Mark but his gesture—I do use to observe
32The state he keeps in getting up.

PEREGRINE

The state he keeps in getting up. ‘Tis worth it, sir.

VOLPONE

33Most noble gentlemen, and my worthy 34patrons! It may seem strange, that I, your Scoto 35Mantuano, who was ever wont to fix my bank in face of 36the public Piazza, near the shelter of the Portico to the 37Procuratia, should now, after eight months absence 38from this illustrious city of Venice, humbly retire myself 39into an obscure nook of the Piazza.

SIR POLITIC

40Did not I now object the same?

PEREGRINE

Did not I now object the same? Peace, sir.

VOLPONE

41Let me tell you: I am not, as your Lombard 42proverb saith, cold on my feet; or content to part with 43my commodities at a cheaper rate, than I accustomed: 44look not for it. Nor that the calumnious reports of that 45impudent detractor, and shame to our profession 46(Alessandro Buttone, I mean), who gave out, in public, 47I was condemned a sforzato to the galleys, for poisoning 48the cardinal Bembo's... cook, hath at all attached, 49much less dejected me. No, no, worthy gentlemen; to 50tell you true, I cannot endure to see the rabble of these 51ground ciarlitani, that spread their cloaks on the 52pavement, as if they meant to do feats of activity, and 53then come in lamely, with their mouldy tales out of 54Boccacio, like stale Tabarine, the fabulist: some of them 55discoursing their travels, and of their tedious captivity in 56the Turks' galleys, when, indeed, were the truth known, 57they were the Christians' galleys, where very temperately 58they eat bread, and drunk water, as a wholesome 59penance, enjoined them by their confessors, for base 60pilferies.

SIR POLITIC

61Note but his bearing, and contempt of these.

VOLPONE

62These turdy-facy-nasty-paty-lousy-fartical 63rogues, with one poor groat's-worth of unprepared 64antimony, finely wrapped up in several scartoccios, are 65able, very well, to kill their twenty a week, and play; yet, 66these meagre, starved spirits, who have half stopped the 67organs of their minds with earthy oppilations, want not 68their favourers among your shrivelled salad-eating 69artisans, who are overjoyed that they may have their 70half-pe'rth of physic; though it purge them into 71another world, it makes no matter.

SIR POLITIC

72Excellent! Have you heard better language, sir?

VOLPONE

73Well, let them go. And, gentlemen, 74honourable gentlemen, know, that for this time, our 75bank, being thus removed from the clamours of the 76canaglia, shall be the scene of pleasure and delight; for 77I have nothing to sell, little or nothing to sell.

SIR POLITIC

78I told you, sir, his end.

PEREGRINE

I told you, sir, his end. You did so, sir.

VOLPONE

79I protest, I, and my six servants, are not able 80to make of this precious liquor, so fast as it is fetched 81away from my lodging by gentlemen of your city; 82strangers of the terra-firma; worshipful merchants; aye, 83and senators too: who, ever since my arrival, have 84detained me to their uses, by their splendidous 85liberalities. And worthily; for, what avails your rich man 86to have his magazines stuffed with moscadelli, or of 87the purest grape, when his physicians prescribe him, on 88pain of death, to drink nothing but water cocted with 89aniseeds? O, health! Health! The blessing of the rich! the 90riches of the poor! Who can buy thee at too dear a rate, 91since there is no enjoying this world without thee? Be 92not then so sparing of your purses, honourable 93gentlemen, as to abridge the natural course of life –

PEREGRINE

94You see his end.

SIR POLITIC

You see his end. Aye, is’t not good?

VOLPONE

95For, when a humid flux, or catarrh, by the 96mutability of air, falls from your head into an arm or 97shoulder, or any other part; take you a ducat, or your 98cecchine of gold, and apply to the place affected: see 99what good effect it can work. No, no, 'tis this blessed 100unguento, this rare extraction, that hath only power to 101disperse all malignant humours, that proceed either of 102hot, cold, moist, or windy causes –

PEREGRINE

103I would he had put in dry too.

SIR POLITIC

I would he had put in dry too. Pray you, observe.

VOLPONE

104To fortify the most indigest and crude 105stomach, aye, were it of one that, through extreme 106weakness, vomited blood, applying only a warm napkin 107to the place, after the unction and fricace;— for the 108vertigine in the head, putting but a drop into your 109nostrils, likewise behind the ears; a most sovereign and 110approved remedy: the mal caduco, cramps, convulsions, 111paralyses, epilepsies, tremor-cordia, retired nerves, ill 112vapours of the spleen, stopping of the liver, the stone, 113the strangury, hernia ventosa, iliaca passio; stops a 114dysenteria immediately; easeth the torsion of the small 115guts; and cures melancholia hypocondriaca, being taken 116and applied according to my printed receipt. 117(Pointing to his bill and his glass) For, this is the physician, this the 118medicine; this counsels, this cures; this gives the 119direction, this works the effect; and, in sum, both 120together may be termed an abstract of the theoric and 121practic in the Aesculapian art. 'Twill cost you eight 122crowns. And,—Zan Fritada, prithee sing a verse 123extempore in honour of it.

SIR POLITIC

124How do you like him, sir?

PEREGRINE

How do you like him, sir? Most strangely, I!

SIR POLITIC

125Is not his language rare?

PEREGRINE

Is not his language rare? But alchemy,
126I never heard the like; or Broughton’s books.

SONG

NANO

1Had old Hippocrates or Galen,
2(That to their books put med’cines all in,)
3But known this secret, they had never
4(Of which they will be guilty ever)
5Been murderers of so much paper,
6Or wasted many a hurtless taper;
7No Indian drug has e’er been famed,
8Tobacco, sassafras not named;
9Ne yet, of guacum one small stick, sir,
10Nor Raymond Lully’s great elixir.
11Ne had been known the Danish Gonswart
12Or Paracelsus, with his long sword.

PEREGRINE

13All, this, yet, will not do; eight crowns is high.

VOLPONE

14No more. Gentlemen, if I had but time to 15discourse to you the miraculous effects of this my oil, 16surnamed Oglio del Scoto; with the countless catalogue 17of those I have cured of the aforesaid, and many more 18diseases; the patents and privileges of all the princes and 19commonwealths of Christendom; or but the depositions 20of those that appeared on my part, before the Signiory 21of the Sanita and most learned College of Physicians; 22where I was authorized, upon notice taken of the 23admirable virtues of my medicaments, and mine own 24excellency in matter of rare and unknown secrets, not 25only to disperse them publicly in this famous city, but 26in all the territories, that happily joy under the govern- 27ment of the most pious and magnificent states of Italy. 28But may some other gallant fellow say, O, there be 29diverse that make profession to have as good, and as 30experimented receipts as yours: indeed, very many have 31assayed, like apes, in imitation of that, which is really 32and essentially in me, to make of this oil; bestowed great 33cost in furnaces, stills, alembics, continual fires, and 34preparation of the ingredients (as indeed there goes to it 35six hundred several simples, besides some quantity of 36human fat, for the conglutination, which we buy of the 37anatomists), but, when these practitioners come to the 38last decoction, blow, blow, puff, puff, and all flies in 39fumo: ha, ha, ha! Poor wretches! I rather pity their folly 40and indiscretion, than their loss of time and money; for 41these may be recovered by industry: but to be a fool 42born, is a disease incurable. For myself, I always from 43my youth have endeavoured to get the rarest secrets, and 44book them, either in exchange, or for money; I spared 45nor cost nor labour, where anything was worthy to be 46learned. And, gentlemen, honourable gentlemen, I will 47undertake, by virtue of chemical art, out of the honour- 48able hat that covers your head, to extract the four 49elements; that is to say, the fire, air, water, and earth, 50and return you your felt without burn or stain. For, 51whilst others have been at the Balloo, I have been at my 52book; and am now past the craggy paths of study, and 53come to the flowery plains of honour and reputation.

SIR POLITIC

54I do assure you, sir, that is his aim.

VOLPONE

55But to our price-

PEREGRINE

But to our price- And that withal, Sir Politic.

VOLPONE

56You all know, honourable gentlemen, I 57never valued this ampulla, or vial, at less than eight 58crowns; but for this time, I am content to be deprived of 59it for six: six crowns is the price, and less in courtesy I 60know you cannot offer me; take it or leave it, 61howsoever, both it and I am at your service. I ask you 62not as the value of the thing, for then I should demand 63of you a thousand crowns, so the Cardinals Montalto, 64Fernese, the great Duke of Tuscany, my gossip, with 65diverse other princes, have given me; but I despise 66money. Only to show my affection to you, honourable 67gentlemen, and your illustrious state here, I have 68neglected the messages of these princes, mine own 69offices, framed my journey hither, only to present you 70with the fruits of my travels. Tune your voices once 71more to the touch of your instruments, and give the 72honourable assembly some delightful recreation.

PEREGRINE

73What monstrous and most painful circumstance
74Is here, to get some three or four gazets,
75Some three-pence, in the whole! for that ‘twill come to.

(Song)

NANO

1You that would last long, list to my song,
2Make no more coil, but buy of this oil.
3Would you be ever fair and young?
4Stout of teeth, and strong of tongue?
5Tart of palate? quick of ear?
6Sharp of sight? of nostril clear?
7Moist of hand? and light of foot?
8Or, I will come nearer to't,
9Would you live free from all diseases?
10Do the act your mistress pleases,
11Yet fright all aches from your bones?
12Here's a medicine, for the nones.

VOLPONE

13Well, I am in a humour at this time to make 14a present of the small quantity my coffer contains; to the 15rich in courtesy, and to the poor for God's sake. 16Wherefore now mark: I asked you six crowns; and six 17crowns, at other times, you have paid me; you shall not 18give me six crowns, nor five, nor four, nor three, nor 19two, nor one; nor half a ducat; no, nor a moccenigo. 20Six–pence it will cost you, or six hundred pound 21–expect no lower price, for, by the banner of my front, 22I will not bate a bagatine, —that I will have, only, a 23pledge of your loves, to carry something from amongst 24you, to show I am not contemned by you. Therefore, 25now, toss your handkerchiefs, cheerfully, cheerfully; and 26be advertised, that the first heroic spirit that deigns to 27grace me with a handkerchief, I will give it a little 28remembrance of something, beside, shall please it better, 29than if I had presented it with a double pistolet.

PEREGRINE

30Will you be that heroic spark, Sir Politic?
31[Celia throws down her handkerchief from the window above]. O, see! The window has prevented you.

VOLPONE

32Lady, I kiss your bounty; and, for this timely 33grace you have done your poor Scoto of Mantua, I will 34return you, over and above my oil, a secret of that high 35and inestimable nature, shall make you for ever 36enamoured on that minute, wherein your eye first 37descended on so mean, yet not altogether to be despised, 38an object. Here is a powder concealed in this paper, of 39which, if I should speak to the worth, nine thousand 40volumes were but as one page, that page as a line, that 41line as a word; so short is this pilgrimage of man (which 42some call life) to the expressing of it. Would I reflect on 43the price? Why, the whole world is but as an empire, 44that empire as a province, that province as a bank, that 45bank as a private purse to the purchase of it. I will only 46tell you; it is the powder that made Venus a goddess 47(given her by Apollo), that kept her perpetually young, 48cleared her wrinkles, firmed her gums, filled her skin, 49coloured her hair; from her derived to Helen, and at the 50sack of Troy unfortunately lost: till now, in this our age, 51it was as happily recovered, by a studious antiquary, out 52of some ruins of Asia, who sent a moiety of it to the 53court of France (but much sophisticated), wherewith the 54ladies there, now, colour their hair. The rest, at this 55present, remains with me; extracted to a quintessence: so 56that, wherever it but touches, in youth it perpetually 57preserves, in age restores the complexion; seats your 58teeth, did they dance like virginal jacks, firm as a wall; 59makes them white as ivory, that were black as –

(Enter Corvino.)

1Spite o’the devil, and my shame! Come down here;

7Heart! ere tomorrow I shall be new-christened,

9About the town.

13This three weeks, all my advices, all my letters.

Best have a care. Nay, so I will. This knight,
16I may not lose him, for my mirth, till night.

ACT 2, SCENE 4

(Enter Volpone, Mosca.)

VOLPONE

1O, I am wounded!

MOSCA

O, I am wounded! Where, sir?

VOLPONE

O, I am wounded! Where, sir? Not without;
2Those blows were nothing: I could bear them ever.
3But angry Cupid, bolting from her eyes,
4Hath shot himself into me like a flame;
5Where, now, he flings about his burning heat,
6As in a furnace an ambitious fire,
7Whose vent is stopped. The fight is all within me.
8I cannot live, except thou help me, Mosca;
9My liver melts, and I, without the hope
10Of some soft air, from her refreshing breath,
11Am but a heap of cinders.

MOSCA

Am but a heap of cinders. ‘Las, good sir,
12Would you had never seen her!

Would you had never seen her! Nay, would thou
13Hads’t never told me of her!

MOSCA

Hads’t never told me of her! Sir, ‘tis true;
14I do confess I was unfortunate,
15And you unhappy: but I’m bound in conscience,
16No less than duty, to effect my best
17To your release of torment, and I will, sir.

VOLPONE

18Dear Mosca, shall I hope?

MOSCA

Dear Mosca, shall I hope? Sir, more than dear,
19I will not bid you to despair of aught
20Within a human compass.

VOLPONE

Within a human compass. O, there spoke
21My better angel, Mosca, take my keys,

MOSCA

25Use but your patience.

Use but your patience. So I have.

Use but your patience. So I have. I doubt not
26To bring success to your desires.

To bring success to your desires. Nay, then,

MOSCA

28If you can horn him, sir, you need not.

If you can horn him, sir, you need not. True;
29Besides, I never meant him for my heir.
30Is not the colour of my beard and eyebrows
31To make me known?

MOSCA

To make me known? No jot.

VOLPONE

To make me known? No jot. I did it well.

MOSCA

32So well, would I could follow you in mine,
33With half the happiness! —and yet I would

Escape your epilogue. But were they gulled

MOSCA

With a belief that I was Scoto? Sir,

ACT 2, SCENE 5

[Enter Corvino, Celia.)

CORVINO

1Death of mine honour, with the city’s fool!
2A juggling, tooth-drawing, prating mountebank!
3And at a public window! where, whilst he,
4With his strained action, and his dole of faces,
5To his drug-lecture draws your itching ears,
6A crew of old, unmarried, noted lechers,
7Stood leering up like satyrs; and you smile
8Most graciously, and fan your favours forth,
9To give your hot spectators satisfaction!
10What, was your mountebank their call? Their whistle?
11Or were you enamoured on his copper rings,
12His saffron jewel, with the toad-stone in’t?
13Or his embroidered suit, with the cope-stitch,
14Made of a hearse cloth? Or his old tilt-feather?
15Or his starched beard? Well, you shall have him, yes!
16He shall come home, and minister unto you
17The fricace for the mother. Or, let me see,
18I think you’d rather mount; would you not mount?
19Why, if you’ll mount, you may; yes, truly, you may:
20And so you may be seen, down to the foot.
21Get you a cittern, Lady Vanity,
22And be a dealer with the virtuous man;
23Make one: I’ll but protest myself a cuckold
24And save your dowry. I’m a Dutchman, I!
25For, if you thought me an Italian,
26You would be damned, ere you did this, you whore!
27Thou’Idst tremble, to imagine that the murder
28Of father, mother, brother, all thy race,
29Should follow, as the subject of my justice.

CELIA

30Good sir, have patience.

CORVINO

Good sir, have patience. What couldst thou propose
31Less to thyself than, in this heat of wrath
32And stung with my dishonor, I should strike

[draws his sword]

33This steel unto thee, with as many stabs

CELIA

35Alas, sir, be appeased! I could not think
36My being at the window should more now
37Move your impatience, than at other times.

CORVINO

38No! not to seek and entertain a parley
39With a known knave, before a multitude!
40You were an actor with your handkerchief,
41Which he most sweetly kissed in the receipt,
42And might, no doubt, return it with a letter,
43And ‘point the place where you might meet; your sister’s,
44Your mother’s, or your aunt’s might serve the turn.

CELIA

45Why, dear sir, when do I make these excuses,
46Or ever stir abroad but to the church?
47And that so seldom–

CORVINO

And that so seldom– Well, it shall be less;
48And thy restraint before was liberty,
49To what I now decree: and therefore mark me.
50First, I will have this bawdy light dammed up;
51And, till’t be done, some two or three yards off,
52I’ll chalk a line, o’er which if thou but chance
53To set thy desperate foot, more hell, more horror,
54More wild remorseless rage shall seize on thee,
55Than on a conjuror, that had heedless left
56His circle’s safety ere his devil was laid.
57Then here’s a lock which I will hang upon thee,
58And, now I think on’t, I will keep thee backwards;
59Thy lodging shall be backwards, thy walks backwards;
60Thy prospect, all be backwards; and no pleasure,
61That thou shalt know but backwards: nay, since you force
62My honest nature, know it is your own,
63Being too open, makes me use you thus:
64Since you will not contain your subtle nostrils
65In a sweet room, but they must snuff the air
66Of rank and sweaty passengers–
Of rank and sweaty passengers– [Knocking.] One knocks.
67Away, and be not seen, pain of thy life;
68Not look toward the window. If thou dost–
69Nay stay, hear this–let me not prosper, whore,
70But I will make thee an anatomy,
71Dissect thee mine own self, and read a lecture
72Upon thee to the city, and in public.
73Away!
Away! [Exit Celia.] Who’s there?

[Enter Servitore]

SERVANT

Away! [Exit Celia.] Who’s there? ‘Tis Signor Mosca, sir.

ACT 2, SCENE 6

CORVINO

1Let him come in. His master’s dead: there’s yet
2Some good to help the bad.-

3I guess your news.

MOSCA

CORVINO

4Is’t not his death?

5Not his recovery?

Not his recovery? Yes, sir. I am cursed,

8Why, sir, with Scoto’s oil;

11Death! That damned mountebank; but for the law,

MOSCA

26And since, to seem the more officious
27And flattering of his health, there, they have had,
28At extreme fees, the College of Physicians
29Consulting on him, how they might restore him;
30Where one would have a cataplasm of spices,

37And to this service, most unhappily,

39Which here I thought to pre-acquaint you with,
40For your advice, since it concerns you most;
41Because, I would not do that thing might cross
42Your ends, on whom I have my whole dependence, sir:
43Yet, if I do it not, they may delate
44My slackness to my patron, work me out
45Of his opinion; and there all your hopes,
46Ventures, or whatsoever, are all frustrate!

CORVINO

Prevent them if you can. Death to my hopes!
51This is my villainous fortune! Best to hire

MOSCA

Some common courtesan? Aye, I thought on that, sir;
53But they are all so subtle, full of art—
54And age again doting and flexible,
55So as–I cannot tell–we may, perchance,
56Light on a quean may cheat us all.

CORVINO

Light on a quean may cheat us all. ‘Tis true.

MOSCA

62How!

MOSCA

CORVINO

63His daughter?

MOSCA

69I pray thee give me leave. [Walks aside.] If any man

MOSCA

75[Aside] I hear him coming.aparte

CORVINO

[Aside] I hear him coming. She shall do’t: ‘tis done.
76‘Slight! if this doctor, who is not engaged,

MOSCA

81How, sir?

CORVINO

How, sir? We’ll make all sure. The party you wot of

MOSCA

Shall be mine own wife, Mosca. Sir, the thing
83But that I would not seem the counsel you
84I should have motioned to you, at the first:
85And make your count, you have cut all their throats.
86Why, ‘tis directly taking a possession!
87And in his next fit, we may let him go.
88‘Tis but to pull the pillow from his head,

CORVINO

But for your scrupulous doubts. Aye, a plague on’t,

MOSCA

Mine own free motion. Sir, I warrant you,
97I’ll so possess him with it, that the rest

CORVINO

102But do not you forget to send now.

MOSCA

But do not you forget to send now. Fear not.

ACT 2, SCENE 7

CORVINO

1Where are you, wife? my Celia! wife!
Where are you, wife? my Celia! wife! [Enter Celia.] —What, blubbering?
2Come, dry those tears. I think thou thought’st me in earnest;
3Ha! By this light I talked so but to try thee.
4Methinks the lightness of the occasion.
5Should have confirmed thee. Come, I am not jealous.

CELIA

6No!

CORVINO

No! Faith I am not, I, nor never was;
7It is a poor unprofitable humour.
8Do not I know, if women have a will,
9They’ll do ‘gainst all the watches of the world,
10And that the fiercest spies are tamed with gold?
11Tut, I am confident in thee, thou shalt see’t;

13Come kiss me. Go, and make thee ready, straight,
14In all thy best attire, thy choicest jewels,

18How fair I am free from jealousy or fear.

ACT 3

SCENE 1

[Enter Mosca.]

MOSCA

1I fear, I shall begin to grow in love
2With my dear self, and most prosperous parts,
3They do so spring and burgeon; I can feel
4A whimsy in my blood: I know not how,
5Success hath made me wanton. I could skip
6Out of my skin, now, like a subtle snake,
7I am so limber. O! your parasite
8Is a most precious thing, dropt from above,
9Not bred ‘mongst clods and clotpoles, here on earth.
10I muse, the mystery was not made a science,
11It is so liberally professed! Almost
12All the wise world is little else, in nature,
13But parasites or sub-parasites. And yet,
14I mean not those that have your bare town-art,
15To know who’s fit to feed them; have no house,
16No family, no care, and therefore mould
17Tales for men’s ears, to bait that sense; or get
18Kitchen-invention, and some stale receipts
19To please the belly, and the groin; nor those,
20With their court dog-tricks, that can fawn and fleer,
21Make their revenue out of legs and faces,
22Echo my lord, and lick away a moth:
23But your fine elegant rascal, that can rise,
24And stoop, almost together, like an arrow,
25Shoot through the air as nimbly as a star;
26Turn short as doth a swallow, and be here
27And there, and here, and yonder, all at once;
28Present to any humour, all occasion;
29And change a visor, swifter than a thought!
30This is the creature had the art born with him;
31Toils not to learn it, but doth practice it
32Out of most excellent nature: and such sparks
33Are the true parasites, others but their zanies.

ACT 3, SCENE 2

[Enter Bonario.]

MOSCA

1Who’s this? Bonario, old Corbaccio’s son?

leave me: I would be loath to interchange discourse

[Weeps.]

BONARIO

18What! does he weep? the sign is soft and good:

26Base offices in rending friends asunder,
27Dividing families, betraying counsels,
28Whispering false lies, or mining men with praises,
29Trained their credulity with perjuries,
30Corrupted chastity, or am in love

MOSCA

38Sir, it concerns you; and though I may seem

41Yet, for the pure love, which I bear all right

43This very hour your father is in purpose

BONARIO

To disinherit you– How!

MOSCA

To disinherit you– How! And thrust you forth,
45As a mere stranger to his blood. ‘tis true, sir.
46The work no way engageth me, but, as

BONARIO

51This tale hath lost thee much of the late trust

53I know not how to lend it any thought,

MOSCA

55It is a confidence that well becomes,
56Your piety; and formed, no doubt, it is

60It is or will be doing; and if you

62I dare not say where you shall see, but where

66Sir, if I do it not, draw your just sword

BONARIO

Weeps blood in anguish– Lead. I follow thee.

ACT 3, SCENE 3

(Enter Volpone, Nano, Androgyno, and Castrone)

NANO

3Dwarf, fool, and eunuch, well met here we be.

(Enter Mosca)
